blocks.text: 今天是 Anthropic 的全新起点：一场酝酿多年的 IPO 终于落地，募资 813 亿美元，超越 SpaceX 成为史上估值最高的 IPO，也为后续其他公开上市的 AI 实验室立下了重要先例。但这不只是一次财务上的里程碑。

inlines.text: 今天是 Anthropic 的全新起点：一场酝酿多年的 IPO 终于落地，募资 813 亿美元，超越 SpaceX 成为史上估值最高的 IPO，也为后续其他公开上市的 AI 实验室立下了重要先例。但这不只是一次财务上的里程碑。

blocks.text: Anthropic 创立时的理念，是把安全放在比其他实验室更优先的位置；其创始人此前都在 OpenAI 担任研究高管。然而随着 AI 竞赛加速，公司高管反复强调，Anthropic 只有拿下第一名，才能真正完成这一使命，而这需要大量资金和算力。不出所料，深思熟虑、安全且审慎的 AI 开发，与赢得这场竞赛所需的极致速度之间，难免产生冲突。再加上 IPO，事情只会更复杂，而 Anthropic 的领导层几乎可以单方面推进这一切。这得益于一种旨在让公司免受股东盈利压力影响的企业架构——但这一架构同时也移除了对其权力的常规制衡。

blocks.text: 一位在 IPO 前离职的 Anthropic 前员工表示，他和公司里的其他人越来越觉得，当前的 AI 开发节奏“在正常的市场结构下难以为继”，尤其是在这样一个影响力巨大、却几乎不受监管的行业里，各方激励本就错位。

blocks.text: 多年来，Anthropic 一直对外宣称自己与其他 AI 公司不同、更为谨慎。理论上，这一点也体现在它的上市方案里。它注册为公益公司（Public Benefit Corporation），这意味着 Anthropic 董事会有责任在使命与股东财富最大化之间取得平衡。正如我的同事 Robert Hart 此前讨论过的，它还设计了一套极不寻常的权力结构。

blocks.text: Anthropic 于2023 年设立的长期利益信托（LTBT）及其创始人掌握着控制性投票权，这意味着即便公司已经上市，股东也永远无法把他们投票赶下台。一种特殊的 T 类股票，让一小群受托人——即 LTBT 成员——拥有“挑选和罢免部分”Anthropic 董事的“权力”。他们不受典型股东压力的影响，理论上是对创始人的一种制衡，其使命是“在预期我们的决策后果将远远超出 Anthropic 本身的关键节点，平衡股东的财务利益与我们的公共利益目标”。

设立的长期利益信托（LTBT）及其创始人掌握着控制性投票权，这意味着即便公司已经上市，股东也永远无法把他们投票赶下台。一种特殊的 T 类股票，让一小群受托人——即 LTBT 成员——拥有“挑选和罢免部分”Anthropic 董事的“权力”。他们不受典型股东压力的影响，理论上是对创始人的一种制衡，其使命是“在预期我们的决策后果将远远超出 Anthropic 本身的关键节点，平衡股东的财务利益与我们的公共利益目标”。

blocks.text: 现实要复杂得多。举例来说，LTBT 在技术上负责选出 Anthropic 七人董事会中的四名成员，但这四人中有一人实际上需要得到 Anthropic 创始人的认可，因此该信托并未掌握直接的多数控制权。此外，关于提名或罢免董事还有附加规定：LTBT 必须提前 30 天通知公司的“提名与公司治理委员会”其决定，该委员会由三名成员组成：联合创始人 Daniela Amodei（担任委员会主席）、Netflix 联合创始人 Reed Hastings，以及 Anthropic 投资人 Yasmin Razavi。

blocks.text: 虽然长期利益信托（LTBT）的成员在公司中“没有经济利益”，但理论上，Anthropic 也完全可以挖走一名受托人，用高薪把他招进公司。马里亚诺-弗洛伦蒂诺·奎利亚尔（前受托人）就在今年 8 月加入 Anthropic，出任首席全球事务官；OpenAI 过去也曾把前董事会成员菲吉·西莫招入公司担任高管。非营利 AI 行业监督机构 The Midas Project 的创始人泰勒·约翰斯顿说，可以设想这样一种情形：如果某位受托人“显得有点太激进之类的，他们大可以直接给这名受托人开出一个条件，用数百万美元的实际报酬换他退出信托，这就是他们对信托施加某种监督的方式之一”。

blocks.text: 尽管 LTBT 被宣传为制衡 Anthropic 领导层的一种手段，但在一些外部观察者看来，细则并不可靠。“这个信托既然在 Anthropic 没有经济利益，理论上可以动用它任命四名董事中三名的权力，让公司不偏离使命，”科罗拉多大学法学院法学教授、公司治理专家安·利普顿说，“但人们有理由怀疑这有多大可能发生。”

blocks.text: 此外，利普顿还质疑：即便信托拥有这样的权力，它是否具备足够的认知来判断何时该对公司的某项计划或产品踩刹车。公开列出的四名 LTBT 成员并非知名的 AI 专家：前美联储主席本·伯南克、外交政策分析师理查德·方丹、实验物理学家克里斯托弗·斯塔布斯，以及曾任 GiveWell 高管的尼尔·巴迪·沙阿——他是 LTBT 主席。“我不认为这些受托人，或者他们任命的董事，对 AI 和 AI 开发有足够的洞察力来做出这些选择，”利普顿说，“他们都是很有声望的人，但本·伯南克对 AI 又了解多少呢？”

blocks.text: 多位专家把 Anthropic 的 LTBT 比作奥特曼被罢免前的 OpenAI 非营利董事会：“长期利益信托的权力——或者说它缺乏的权力……在某些方面类似于 OpenAI 非营利组织拥有的权力，”The Midas Project 的约翰斯顿说。当然，那个董事会罢免 OpenAI CEO 萨姆·奥特曼的决定，最终在几天后导致奥特曼回归担任 CEO，董事会多数成员辞职并被替换。

blocks.text: Anthropic 成为上市公司后，在获取资本方面将面临前所未有的更大压力，无论是靠提高营收还是靠融资。这意味着，正如多年来行业内的一贯趋势，那些昂贵的 AI 安全举措将越来越难以证明其合理性，加快产品发布和商业化的压力也必然加大。“这个信托和创始人加在一起，才是真正掌握治理权的一方，”Lipton 说。“所以你要么相信他们会妥善平衡社会利益，要么不信。无论哪种情况，他们即便有社会层面的意愿，真正的制约都将是 Anthropic 需要钱这一事实。”

blocks.text: Anthropic 的网站总结该公司的存在理由为一件事：“将安全置于前沿的 AI 研究与产品。”但同样清楚的是，要让这一安全承诺真正有意义，Anthropic 需要大量资源才能维持业务的存续。与其他实验室一样，它一直在追求递归式自我改进——这是一个颇具争议且可能危险的行业里程碑，指的是 AI 系统能够自主改进并创造出自身的高级版本。“你无法从第二名做到安全，”Anthropic 政策主管 Sarah Heck 在九月表示。

blocks.text: 周三，人工智能安全中心发布了一份新声明，Hugging Face、哈佛大学等机构的知名业内人士联署。声明指称Anthropic“不是一家安全的人工智能公司”，并称其试图“以增进公共利益之名聚敛权力”。声明写道：“Anthropic警告说，递归自我改进的人工智能可能集中权力、脱离人类控制，自己却抢先把它造出来。公司用安全标签招揽投资者、员工和公众——与此同时，它悄悄弱化了自己的安全承诺，还游说推动有利于自己的监管。”

blocks.text: Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone.

inlines.text: Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone.

blocks.text: Anthropic was founded on the idea that it prioritized safety more than other labs; its founders had left executive research positions at OpenAI. As the AI race has accelerated, though, its executives have emphasized that Anthropic can only fulfill this mission by coming in first place, requiring lots of money and compute. Unsurprisingly, thoughtful, safe, and intentional AI development can conflict with the kind of sheer speed that winning this race requires. Adding in an initial public offering only complicates things further, and Anthropic’s leadership can pursue it more or less unilaterally. That’s thanks to a corporate structure focused on insulating the company from shareholder pressure to turn a profit — but one that also removes typical checks on its power.

blocks.text: One former Anthropic employee, who left ahead of the IPO, said he and others at Anthropic have increasingly been feeling that the current pace of AI development is “untenable under normal market structures,” particularly with the mismatched incentives at play in a powerful industry with little to no oversight.

blocks.text: Anthropic has spent years billing itself as different from, and more careful than, other AI companies. In theory, this extends to its plan for going public. It’s registered as a Public Benefit Corporation, which means Anthropic’s board has a responsibility to balance its mission against shareholder wealth maximization. As my colleague Robert Hart has discussed before, it has also developed a highly unusual power structure.

blocks.text: Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), introduced in 2023, and its founders have controlling voting rights, meaning they’d never be able to be voted out by shareholders even as a public company. A special class of stock, Class T, allows a small group of trustees — the members of the LTBT — the “authority to select and remove a portion of” Anthropic’s board. They exist outside typical shareholder pressure and theoretically are a check for the founders, tasked with a mission to “balance the financial interests of our stockholders and our public benefit purpose at key junctures where we expect the consequences of our decisions to reach far beyond Anthropic.”

blocks.text: The reality is significantly more complicated. The LTBT technically chooses four members of Anthropic’s seven-person board, for instance, but one of those four effectively needs to be approved by Anthropic’s founders, leaving the trust short of straightforward majority control. There are also stipulations about nominating or removing a director: the LTBT must provide its decision with 30 days’ notice to the company’s “nominating and corporate governance committee,” which consists of three members: co-founder Daniela Amodei (who is chair of the committee), Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, and Anthropic investor Yasmin Razavi.

blocks.text: Though the LTBT members are “financially disinterested” in the company, there’s also nothing stopping Anthropic from hypothetically hiring away a trustee and paying them a lot of money to work for the company. Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar (a former trustee) joined Anthropic in August as its Chief Global Affairs Officer, and OpenAI has in the past hired a former board member, Fidji Simo, to an executive position within the company. One could imagine a scenario in which, if a trustee was “looking a little bit too activist-y or something, they could just make that trustee an offer with millions of dollars in effective compensation that would entail stepping down from the trust, and that’s one way that they could have some oversight over this,” said Tyler Johnston, founder of The Midas Project, a nonprofit AI industry watchdog.

blocks.text: Although the LTBT is billed as a way to check Anthropic’s leadership, to some outside observers, the fine print looks shaky. “The trust, since it doesn’t have a financial interest in Anthropic, could theoretically use its power with three slash four directors to keep the company on mission,” says Ann Lipton, law professor at the University of Colorado Law School and an expert in corporate governance. “One might question how likely that is to occur.”

blocks.text: Moreover, Lipton questions whether the trust would know enough to gauge when to hit the brakes on a company plan or product even if they did have such authority. The four listed LTBT members aren’t known to be AI experts: they include former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke, foreign policy analyst Richard Fontaine, experimental physicist Christopher Stubbs, and former GiveWell executive Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT. “I’m not convinced that the trustees or the directors that they appoint have the insight into AI and AI development to be able to make these choices,” Lipton says. “They’re very prestigious people, but what does Ben Bernanke know about AI?”

blocks.text: Several experts compared Anthropic’s LTBT to OpenAI’s nonprofit board before Altman’s ouster: “The powers, or lack thereof, of the Long-Term Benefit Trust … [are] analogous in some ways to the powers that the OpenAI nonprofit has,” said The Midas Project’s Johnston. Of course, that board’s decision to oust OpenAI CEO Sam Altman ended up leading, days later, to Altman’s return as CEO and the majority of the board’s resignation and replacement.

Of course, that board’s decision to oust OpenAI CEO Sam Altman ended up leading, days later, to Altman’s return as CEO and the majority of the board’s resignation and replacement.

blocks.text: But there’s a notable difference between that and the LTBT. Before OpenAI’s restructuring, its nonprofit board had the ability to step in and guide day-to-day decisions at the company when deemed necessary, and even after its restructuring, they retained that ability for safety and security matters, such as delaying or stopping a model release. Anthropic’s Form S-1 suggests that the LTBT, with its main duty being appointing (and potentially removing) certain board members, does not have either of those levels of authority.

blocks.text: The former Anthropic employee said that Anthropic’s founders are essentially the only ones with any real decisionmaking power: “I would be surprised if you could find anyone who knows the founders, knows the Long-Term Benefit Trust, understands how decisions get made, and thinks the Long-Term Benefit Trust has any meaningful power,” he said. The employee added that the trustees were both “poorly equipped to provide meaningful oversight” to the founders and also selected on purpose to not rock the boat.

blocks.text: Anthropic as a public company will face more pressure than ever before to secure capital, whether via driving more revenue or fundraising. That means that, as has been a trend in the industry for years, it will likely be more difficult to justify expensive AI safety initiatives, and there will inevitably be more pressure to speed up product releases and commercialization. “This trust and the founders together are the ones who actually have governance power,” Lipton said. “So you either trust that they are going to balance the interests of society appropriately, or you don’t. Either way, the real constraint on whatever societal impulses they have is going to be the fact that Anthropic needs money.”

blocks.text: Anthropic has been open about the fact that it’s in extreme need of cold, hard cash, particularly to buy more compute and speed up its AI advancement. “Compute is the deepest business dilemma that the company faces,” Amodei said last Friday in a livestreamed conversation with JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. “If you buy too much, of course you can financially overextend yourself. If you buy too little, then you can’t support inference for customers, and even more importantly … you can’t do the R&D.”

blocks.text: Anthropic’s website summarizes the company’s raison d’être as one thing: “AI research and products that put safety at the frontier.” But it’s also been clear that for that safety pledge to matter, Anthropic needs vast resources to remain a viable business. Like other labs, it’s been pursuing recursive self-improvement, a controversial and potentially dangerous industry milestone denoting AI systems that can autonomously improve and create advanced versions of themselves. “You can’t do safety from second place,” said Anthropic policy chief Sarah Heck in September.

blocks.text: This explanation hasn’t satisfied everyone, including some Anthropic employees. Anthropic’s head of safeguards research departed in February alleging that “the world is in peril”; one of its researchers, Jacob Coxon, made headlines in September for claiming that both Anthropic and OpenAI are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”; and that same month, an Anthropic safety researcher departed for a job at nonprofit third-party AI auditor METR, writing that “AI companies are on track to impose an unprecedented level of risk on society” and that “while Anthropic hasn’t had as severe an incident as the HuggingFace attack [by OpenAI agents], I think that’s partly a matter of luck.”

blocks.text: On Wednesday, a new statement from the Center for AI Safety, with prominent industry signatories from Hugging Face, Harvard University, and more, alleged that Anthropic is “not a safe AI company” and that it attempts to “amass power in the name of the greater good.” It stated, “Anthropic warns that recursively self-improving AI could concentrate power and escape human control, yet races to build it first. The company uses safety branding to court investors, employees, and the public—even as it has quietly weakened its safety pledges and lobbied for self-serving regulation.”

blocks.text: Anthropic’s website states that “at the end of the day, the mission is what we’re all here for. It gives us a shared purpose and allows us to act swiftly together, rather than being pulled in multiple directions by competing goals. It engenders trust and collaboration, and is the final arbiter in our decisions.” The question is whether, and how, the interpretation of Anthropic’s mission may shift — once it’s facing more pressure than ever before to justify a fully diluted market cap of about $1.5 trillion.
